primary_reference.title: SPIA Bangladesh Study 2025: Updating the Green Revolution
primary_reference.authors: Singla, S., Ul Islam, T., Hassan, F., Monteiro, I., Stevenson, J., Emerick, K.
primary_reference.publisher: Standing Panel on Impact Assessment (SPIA), Rome
primary_reference.note: This dashboard presents and verifies a subset of the SPIA 2025 evidence in a navigable form. The canonical source is the SPIA report and its replication repository, both linked below.

institutions.name: CGIAR Standing Panel on Impact Assessment
institutions.role: Funder and steward of the MIXTAPE project and of the 2024 round of the BIHS panel. Country studies, including this Bangladesh study, sit under SPIA's strategic country-studies pillar.

links.title: SPIA Bangladesh Study 2025 (GitHub: code, data structure, codebooks)

institutions.name: Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research
institutions.role: Global research partnership for a food-secure future. The MIXTAPE project assesses adoption and impact of CGIAR-linked innovations in Bangladesh.

institutions.name: International Rice Research Institute
institutions.role: Source of the parent material for almost all BRRI HYV rice releases, including the BR-28 / BR-29 mega-varieties and the Sub1 submergence-tolerance and salinity-tolerance lines released through STRASA.

links.title: STRASA legacy site (Stress-Tolerant Rice for Africa and South Asia)

institutions.name: WorldFish (formerly ICLARM)
institutions.role: CGIAR centre for aquatic foods. Developer of GIFT tilapia, partner on carp polyculture and nutrition-sensitive carp-mola systems, and supporter of Bangladesh's pond aquaculture extension since the 1980s.

institutions.name: International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center
institutions.role: Lead CGIAR centre for the Cereal Systems Initiative for South Asia (CSISA) and CSISA Mechanization Initiative (CSISA-MI). Has scaled the axial-flow pump, power-tiller-operated seeders, reapers and other small-farm machinery in Bangladesh.

institutions.name: HarvestPlus
institutions.role: CGIAR programme for staple-food biofortification. Co-developer with BRRI of the zinc-biofortified BRRI dhan62, 64, 72, 74, 84, 100 (Bangabandhu) and the iron-biofortified pearl-millet and wheat lines tested in Bangladesh.

institutions.name: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute
institutions.role: National rice research institute. Releases all BRRI-prefix and BRRI Dhan-prefix varieties and designs Bangladesh-specific farm machinery (open-drum threshers, mini combines).

institutions.name: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture
institutions.role: National institute for mutation breeding, collaborating with the IAEA and FAO Joint Division. Releases all Binadhan rice varieties including Binadhan-7, 8, 10, 11, 17, 25.

institutions.name: Bangladesh Fisheries Research Institute
institutions.role: National fisheries research institute. Domestic seed-production technology for carps, catfishes (shing/magur) and monosex tilapia, and host of Bangladesh's freshwater fish health labs.

institutions.name: Department of Fisheries, Bangladesh
institutions.role: Government agency overseeing freshwater and marine fisheries extension, hatchery licensing and aquaculture statistics.

institutions.name: International Atomic Energy Agency (FAO Joint Division)
institutions.role: Technical partner for BINA on mutation breeding. The IAEA Mutant Variety Database lists all registered Binadhan releases including Binadhan-25.

institutions.name: International Development Enterprises
institutions.role: Non-profit that mass-marketed the treadle pump in Bangladesh from 1986 (over 1.5 million units sold) and partners with CSISA-MI on axial-flow pump distribution.

technologies.name: Chandina
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Chandina (BR-1), released in 1970, was the first high-yielding variety from BRRI, derived from IRRI semi-dwarf germplasm in the IR8 family. Targeted at the irrigated Boro season with yields around 5.5 t/ha, it was the first IRRI-derived semi-dwarf rice grown at scale in Bangladesh.

sources.title: BRRI varieties (Digital Herbarium of Crop Plants, BSMRAU)

technologies.name: Biplab
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Biplab (BR-3), released in 1973, was BRRI's first variety adapted to all three rice seasons (Aus, Aman, Boro), with yields of roughly 6.5, 4.0 and 4.0 t/ha respectively.

sources.title: BRRI varieties (Digital Herbarium of Crop Plants, BSMRAU)

technologies.name: Mukta
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Mukta (BR-11) is the dominant Transplanted Aman mega-variety in Bangladesh, released in 1980 from a cross between IRRI's IR20 and IR5. It combines high yield (~6.5 t/ha), moderate tungro resistance and yellow stem-borer tolerance, and has anchored monsoon-season rice production for decades alongside BRRI dhan28 and dhan29.

sources.title: Breeding History of Three Mega Rice Varieties (BR11, BRRI dhan28, dhan29)
BRRI varieties (Digital Herbarium of Crop Plants, BSMRAU)

technologies.name: Gazi
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Gazi (BR-14) was released in 1983 for cultivation in both Boro and Aus seasons, yielding around 6.0 t/ha. It expanded BRRI's HYV portfolio into the dry-season irrigated and early-monsoon ecosystems and remained popular for over a decade before BRRI dhan28/29 became dominant.

sources.title: BRRI varieties (Digital Herbarium of Crop Plants, BSMRAU)

technologies.name: Shahi Balam
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Shahi Balam (BR-16), approved by the National Seed Board in 1983, is a Boro/Aus variety descended from IRRI semi-dwarf germplasm and locally adapted Balam landraces. It is known for its medium-bold grain and a notably low glycemic index relative to other BRRI HYVs.

sources.title: BRRI varieties (Digital Herbarium of Crop Plants, BSMRAU)

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 28
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.cgiar_origin: IRRI parent (cross of IR28 x Purbachi)
technologies.type: BRRI core, IRRI-derived HYV, Boro mega-variety
technologies.description: BRRI Dhan 28 is one of the two dominant Boro-season mega-varieties of Bangladesh, released in 1994 from a cross between IRRI's IR28 and the local variety Purbachi. Short-duration (~140 days), semi-dwarf and producing ~6.0 t/ha, it has historically covered along with BRRI Dhan 29 around 70 percent of national Boro area and over 90 percent of the Haor wetlands, although it is now increasingly susceptible to blast and brown plant-hopper.

sources.title: Breeding History of Three Mega Rice Varieties
Mega rice varieties becoming less productive (Dhaka Tribune)

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 29
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.type: BRRI core, IRRI-derived HYV, Boro mega-variety
technologies.description: BRRI Dhan 29 is the highest-yielding Boro mega-variety in Bangladesh (potential ~7.5 t/ha), released in 1994 from a cross between the Sri Lankan IRRI-derived line BG90-2 and Bangladesh's BR10. Longer duration than BRRI Dhan 28 (~160 days), it has co-dominated the irrigated Boro ecosystem since the mid-1990s.

sources.title: Breeding History of Three Mega Rice Varieties

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 39
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Short-duration Transplanted Aman variety released in 1999 with yields around 4.5 t/ha. Its early maturity (~120 days) enables farmers to plant a winter pulse, oilseed or potato crop after harvest, supporting rice-based crop diversification in northern Bangladesh.

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 47 (saline-tolerant Boro)
technologies.developer: BRRI with IRRI
technologies.cgiar_origin: IRRI line IR63307-4B-4-3, selected via Participatory Variety Selection (STRASA)
technologies.description: Salt-tolerant Boro-season variety released in 2007 and derived from IRRI breeding line IR63307-4B-4-3 through participatory variety selection in Bangladesh's coastal districts. Tolerates salinity up to ~12 dS/m at seedling stage and ~8 dS/m at later stages.

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 49
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Widely adopted Transplanted Aman variety released in 2007. Plant height ~100 cm, ~5.5 t/ha yield and a medium-slender grain resembling the popular Naizer Shail type, making it one of the most planted Aman varieties after BR-11.

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 50 (Banglamoti)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Aromatic premium-quality Boro variety branded as Banglamoti, designed as a Basmati-equivalent for Bangladesh. Fine slender grain with distinctive aroma and ~6.0 t/ha yield.

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 51 (Swarna-Sub1)
technologies.developer: BRRI with IRRI
technologies.description: Bangladesh's release of Swarna-Sub1, a submergence-tolerant Aman variety carrying the SUB1A QTL identified by IRRI/UC Davis and introgressed into the Swarna background. Can survive 2 weeks of complete flash flooding, a critical trait for haor and rainfed lowland zones.

sources.title: Adoption of submergence-tolerant BRRI dhan51/52 in northern Bangladesh

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 52 (BR11-Sub1)
technologies.developer: BRRI with IRRI
technologies.description: BR11-Sub1: the SUB1A submergence-tolerance QTL from IRRI introgressed into the country's flagship Aman mega-variety BR-11. Preserves BR-11's agronomy and grain quality while surviving up to ~15 days of complete submergence.

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 58
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: High-yielding Boro variety released in 2012, plant height ~100-105 cm, slightly more slender grain than BRRI Dhan 29 and yield potential 7.0-7.5 t/ha over a 150-155 day cycle. Positioned as a successor to BRRI Dhan 29.

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 62 (Zn-biofortified)
technologies.developer: BRRI with HarvestPlus
technologies.description: The world's first biofortified zinc-enriched rice variety, released in 2013 under the HarvestPlus CGIAR biofortification programme. Short-duration Transplanted Aman (~100 days) containing ~19-20 ppm zinc in the polished grain to address zinc deficiency.

sources.title: HarvestPlus Bangladesh: zinc rice programme overview
SPIA Bangladesh Study 2025, Section 4.1.1 (rice biofortification timeline)

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 64 (Zn-biofortified)
technologies.developer: BRRI with HarvestPlus
technologies.description: Second zinc-biofortified rice from BRRI, approved by the National Seed Board in 2014 under HarvestPlus. Boro season, yield ~6.0 t/ha; grain carries up to ~25 ppm zinc.

sources.title: Another variety of zinc-enriched rice released (Daily Star)

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 66 (drought-tolerant)
technologies.developer: BRRI with IRRI/STRASA
technologies.description: Drought-tolerant Transplanted Aman variety approved in 2014 for Bangladesh's rainfed lowland ecosystem, developed with IRRI under STRASA. Maintains 4.5-5.0 t/ha without irrigation during the reproductive stage in drought-prone Barind and northwest regions.

sources.title: Development of Drought Tolerant BRRI dhan66 (Bangladesh Rice Journal)

technologies.name: BRRI Dhan 67 (saline-tolerant)
technologies.developer: BRRI with IRRI/STRASA
technologies.description: Salinity-tolerant Boro variety released in 2014 under STRASA. 3.8-7.4 t/ha under coastal saline conditions, complements BRRI Dhan 47 across the southern coastal districts.

technologies.name: BRRI dhan71 (drought)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Drought-tolerant Transplanted Aman derived from an IRRI breeding line, surviving up to 28 days of drought at the reproductive stage. ~5.5 t/ha under normal and 3.0-4.0 t/ha under drought, 115-day duration, targeted at rainfed lowland areas of northwest Bangladesh.

technologies.name: BRRI dhan72 (Zn-enriched Aman)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Zinc-enriched Transplanted Aman variety developed with HarvestPlus-CGIAR biofortification efforts, yielding ~5.7 t/ha. One of the earliest zinc-biofortified releases in the Aman season.

technologies.name: BRRI dhan74 (Zn-biofortified)
technologies.developer: BRRI with HarvestPlus
technologies.description: Zinc-biofortified Boro variety yielding around 7.1 t/ha, developed in partnership with HarvestPlus. Part of the BRRI Zn-rice family alongside BRRI dhan84 and BRRI dhan100.

technologies.name: BRRI dhan75 (short Aman)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Short-duration Transplanted Aman variety with medium-coarse white grain, designed for early harvest so farmers can establish a timely rabi (winter) crop such as mustard or potato. ~4.5 t/ha.

technologies.name: BRRI dhan78 (submergence + saline)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Dual-tolerant Transplanted Aman with tolerance to both submergence and salinity at the vegetative stage, particularly valuable for the coastal flood-prone belt. Yields about 4.5-4.7 t/ha.

sources.title: Effect of Degree of Milling on BRRI dhan78 (PMC)

technologies.name: BRRI dhan80 (Jasmine-type aromatic)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Jasmine-type aromatic, long-slender-grain Aman variety positioned as exportable premium quality rice. Plant height ~120 cm with 130-135 days duration; fragrance and grain quality comparable to imported Thai jasmine rice.

sources.title: BRRI dhan80 (European Journal of Nutrition & Food Safety)

technologies.name: BRRI dhan81 (BR-28 replacement)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: High-yielding premium-quality Boro variety with long slender grain, intended as a replacement for the widely grown but aging BRRI dhan28. Yields 6.0-6.5 t/ha with similar duration to BRRI dhan28.

technologies.name: BRRI dhan84 (Zn + Fe biofortified)
technologies.developer: BRRI with HarvestPlus
technologies.description: Zinc and iron biofortified Boro variety developed with HarvestPlus support, yielding 6.0-6.5 t/ha in a 140-145 day duration. Designed to address hidden hunger through staple-food biofortification in the irrigated dry season.

technologies.name: BRRI dhan87 (popular new Aman)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: High-yielding Transplanted Aman with long thin white grain and a 127-day life cycle, yielding around 6.0-6.5 t/ha. Has become one of the most popular new Aman varieties since release.

sources.title: Rice farmers' perception on features of BRRI dhan87 (SAU)

technologies.name: BRRI dhan88 (BR-28 successor)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: High-yielding Transplanted Boro variety developed via anther culture with a 140-143 day duration and yield potential of ~7 t/ha. Positioned as a higher-yielding, more pest-resilient replacement for BRRI dhan28.

sources.title: BRRI dhan88 fact sheet (BRRI Knowledge Bank PDF)

technologies.name: BRRI dhan89 (top-yielding Boro)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.cgiar_origin: Cross with wild rice Oryza rufipogon
technologies.description: Top-yielding Boro variety derived from a cross between BRRI dhan29 and Oryza rufipogon, with a 154-158 day life cycle. Yields around 8 t/ha or more, positioned as a high-yielding replacement for BRRI dhan29.

sources.title: BRRI introduces high-yielding Boro varieties (TBS News)

technologies.name: BRRI dhan92
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI)
technologies.description: Short-statured (~107 cm) Boro variety with long thin grain and a 156-160 day duration, yielding up to 8.4 t/ha. Top yield performer in the Boro season; subject of current marker-assisted breeding work to add blast and bacterial blight resistance.

sources.title: Genetic enhancement of BRRI dhan92 (Tropical Plant Pathology 2025)

technologies.name: BRRI dhan100 (Bangabandhu)
technologies.developer: BRRI with HarvestPlus
technologies.description: Zinc-biofortified Boro variety with 25.6 mg/kg zinc, slender non-sticky grain, 148-day life cycle, and 7.7 t/ha yield. Named for Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's centenary; the 100th BRRI rice release and the headline Zn-rice variety.

technologies.name: Binadhan-7 (Monga-escape Aman)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA)
technologies.description: Short-duration Aman mutant harvested ~1 month earlier than other Aman cultivars, helping northern Bangladesh farmers escape the seasonal Monga food-insecurity period. Developed via gamma-ray mutation with IAEA support, one of the most widely adopted BINA varieties.

sources.title: Bangladesh Triples Rice Production with Nuclear Science (IAEA)

technologies.name: Binadhan-8 (saline Boro)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA)
technologies.description: Salt-tolerant Boro variety bred for the saline coastal belt, tolerating soil salinity ~8-10 dS/m, yielding ~4.5-5.0 t/ha. Key tool for restoring rice production in cyclone- and salinity-affected districts such as Satkhira.

sources.title: Economic Analysis of Binadhan-8 vs BR-28 (Progressive Agriculture)

technologies.name: Binadhan-10 (highly saline)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA)
technologies.description: Highly salt-tolerant Boro variety tolerating salinity up to ~12 dS/m, yielding >5 t/ha in coastal gher (rice-shrimp) systems. Widely promoted in southwestern Bangladesh.

sources.title: Yield Gap of Stress Tolerant Binadhan-10 & 11 (Agricultural Sciences)

technologies.name: Binadhan-11 (submergence Aman)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA)
technologies.description: Submergence-tolerant Aman variety surviving 20-25 days of complete flooding, designed for flash-flood-prone haors and low-lying Aman areas. Short duration (~118 days), >4 t/ha; adopted in eastern India (Odisha) as well.

technologies.name: Binadhan-14 (short Aus)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA)
technologies.description: Short-duration Aus mutant maturing in ~100-105 days with long slender premium grain. Developed in ~4 years using nuclear techniques and helps farmers fit a rice crop into the short pre-monsoon Aus window.

technologies.name: Binadhan-16 (drought Aman)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA)
technologies.description: Very short-duration drought-tolerant Aman (~105 days), allowing early harvest and creating space for a timely rabi crop. Promoted in drought-prone Barind tract districts of northwest Bangladesh.

sources.title: BINA rice varieties for Barind (BSS News)

technologies.name: Binadhan-17 (Green Super Rice)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA)
technologies.cgiar_origin: IAEA/FAO mutation breeding; Green Super Rice (GSR) lineage
technologies.description: Photo-insensitive Green Super Rice Aman mutant requiring ~20 percent less nitrogen and ~30 percent less water, with drought tolerance and yields up to ~5.6 t/ha. Combines high yield with resource-use efficiency.

sources.title: Yield of Binadhan-17 vs BRRI dhan58 (UJEcology)

technologies.name: Binadhan-19 (drought Aus)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA)
technologies.description: Drought-tolerant direct-seeded Aus with short ~100-day duration, evaluated in Pabna, Rajshahi, Chapainawabganj, Mymensingh and Rangpur. Suited to rainfed upland and medium-highland systems.

sources.title: Drought Tolerant Rice in Bangladesh (SAARC J. Agriculture)

technologies.name: Binadhan-25 (premium fine-grain)
technologies.developer: Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA)
technologies.cgiar_origin: IAEA/FAO mutation breeding (registered in IAEA Mutant Variety DB)
technologies.description: Premium fine-grain Aman with average trial yield ~7.6 t/ha and 145-day duration, intended as a high-quality, high-yield alternative to imported fine rice. Promoted in the Barind region.

sources.title: IAEA Mutant Variety Database: Bina dhan 25

technologies.name: Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia (GIFT)
technologies.developer: WorldFish (then ICLARM) with partners from the Philippines (BFAR, UPLB) and Norway (AKVAFORSK)
technologies.description: Selectively bred Nile tilapia developed from 1988 using a pedigree-based combined family selection scheme. Across six generations the strain achieved roughly 85 percent faster growth than the founding base population; gains of 10-15 percent per generation have been documented. GIFT-derived strains now account for ~75 percent of global tilapia production. Brood stock reached Bangladesh through WorldFish's regional dissemination program in the late 1990s.

sources.title: Ponzoni et al. 2011, Reviews in Aquaculture 3:27-41

technologies.name: Nile tilapia (non-improved)
technologies.developer: African cichlid; introduced to Bangladesh in 1974 (Thai stock) and again in 1987
technologies.description: Hardy, fast-growing African cichlid tolerating a wide range of temperatures, salinities and oxygen levels. Non-improved O. niloticus stocks were introduced to Bangladesh in the 1970s-80s and farmed widely before improved strains such as GIFT and BFRI's monosex Abhijat. These unselected lineages still dominate parts of the smallholder hatchery sector but grow 30-60 percent slower than GIFT.

sources.title: FAO Cultured Aquatic Species Fact Sheet: O. niloticus

technologies.name: Carp polyculture system
technologies.species: Multi-species (rohu, catla, mrigal, silver carp, common carp, grass carp; often + mola)
technologies.developer: Indigenous South Asian practice refined by ICAR (India) and BFRI/WorldFish in Bangladesh
technologies.cgiar_origin: WorldFish (Carp-SIS polyculture, Carp Genetic Improvement Program)
technologies.description: Dominant freshwater aquaculture system in Bangladesh. Stocks species that occupy complementary feeding niches: surface (catla, silver carp), column (rohu, grass carp), and bottom (mrigal, common carp) feeders, maximising pond productivity at low feed cost. Carp-mola variant adds small indigenous mola (~15-20 percent of yield by weight) to deliver vitamin A, iron, zinc and calcium-rich fish without reducing carp yield.

technologies.name: Rohu
technologies.developer: Indigenous Indo-Gangetic species; induced breeding by ICAR-CIFRI (1957); selectively bred rohu by WorldFish in Bangladesh (Carp Genetic Improvement Program, 2012+)
technologies.description: The most consumed and highest-value of the three Indian major carps in Bangladesh and the column-feeding cornerstone of carp polyculture. Induced breeding using pituitary extracts in 1957 ended dependence on wild fry. WorldFish's Carp Genetic Improvement Program in Bangladesh has produced selectively bred rohu reportedly growing 25-30 percent faster than unimproved stocks.

sources.title: WorldFish improved carp boosts profits 25 percent

technologies.name: Catla
technologies.developer: Indigenous Indo-Gangetic species; induced breeding refined in India in the late 1950s
technologies.description: Fastest-growing of the three Indian major carps and the surface/zooplankton feeder in the polyculture mix. Propagated in hatcheries via hypophysation since the late 1950s, stocked at 15-20 percent in six-species composite carp culture and at 30-35 percent in three-species culture.

technologies.name: Mrigal
technologies.developer: Indigenous Indo-Gangetic species; induced breeding from late 1950s
technologies.description: Bottom-feeding component of the Indian major carp polyculture, completing the three-niche complementarity with catla (surface) and rohu (column). Endemic to South Asian river systems and propagated by induced spawning; being gradually substituted by common carp in some commercial operations because of faster growth.

sources.title: FAO Inland Fisheries Synopsis 120: C. mrigala

technologies.name: Silver carp
technologies.developer: Native to East Asia; introduced to Bangladesh in 1969 from Hong Kong via India
technologies.description: Exotic Chinese carp introduced to Bangladesh in 1969 to add a phytoplankton-feeding surface dweller to the polyculture mix. Feeds directly on phytoplankton without supplementary feed, making it one of the cheapest and fastest-growing options for smallholders.

technologies.name: Common carp
technologies.developer: Native to Eurasia; mirror and scaled strains introduced to Bangladesh from the 1960s onwards
technologies.description: Omnivorous bottom feeder that breeds naturally in ponds (unlike Indian major carps) and tolerates wide temperature and water-quality ranges. The most important bottom-feeding component in Bangladeshi polyculture after mrigal, increasingly substituting for it. Improved strains from Hungary, Thailand and Vietnam have raised growth performance.

technologies.name: Grass carp
technologies.developer: Native to East Asia; introduced to Bangladesh in 1966 from Hong Kong via India
technologies.description: Macrophyte-feeding Chinese carp that converts terrestrial and aquatic plant material into fish biomass, valuable in integrated pond systems where farmers can supply cut grass, banana leaves and aquatic weeds. Low-input component of six-species carp polyculture, also used for aquatic vegetation control.

technologies.name: Mola (carp-mola polyculture)
technologies.developer: Indigenous small species; carp-mola polyculture developed by WorldFish (Thilsted et al.) with BFRI, BAU and DoF from late 1990s onwards
technologies.description: Small (5-10 cm) freshwater cyprinid eaten whole (bones, head, eyes, viscera included), exceptionally rich in vitamin A (>2,500 ug RE/100 g), calcium, iron and zinc. Pioneering work led by Shakuntala Thilsted and Nanna Roos at WorldFish showed adding mola to existing carp polyculture ponds (~15-20 percent yield share) measurably improves vitamin A status of women and young children without reducing carp output.

technologies.name: Pangas (striped catfish)
technologies.developer: Native to Mekong/Chao Phraya/Ayeyawady basins; seed and grow-out tech developed in Vietnam and Thailand; introduced to Bangladesh from Thailand ~1990
technologies.description: Striped catfish introduced to Bangladesh in the early 1990s; now one of the most important high-volume, low-cost cultured fish, mainly produced in intensive monoculture in Mymensingh using pelleted feed. Fast growth, air-breathing ability and tolerance of high density made it a pillar of the 'quiet revolution' in Bangladeshi aquaculture.

technologies.name: Galda (giant freshwater prawn)
technologies.developer: Native to Indo-West Pacific; hatchery tech developed by Ling and Fujimura in Malaysia/Hawaii (1960s); adapted in Bangladesh from 1980s with WorldFish, BAU, DoF support
technologies.description: The giant freshwater prawn, world's most economically important cultured freshwater crustacean. Farmed primarily in southwestern coastal gher systems often rotated or integrated with rice. Together with bagda one of the country's two principal aquaculture export commodities.

technologies.name: Bagda (black tiger shrimp)
technologies.developer: Native to Indo-West Pacific; commercial coastal farming developed regionally from 1970s-80s; Bangladesh's bagda industry expanded from early 1980s
technologies.description: The black tiger shrimp, the most valuable brackish-water aquaculture species in Bangladesh and a major foreign-exchange source. Cultured extensively in southwestern coastal gher ponds using wild-caught and increasingly hatchery-produced postlarvae. Disease outbreaks (especially WSSV), wild seed dependence, and salinity intrusion have constrained productivity.

technologies.name: Koi (climbing perch)
technologies.developer: Indigenous to South/Southeast Asia; improved Thai and Vietnamese strains introduced to Bangladesh in the 2000s with BFRI propagation and commercial hatchery uptake
technologies.description: Hardy air-breathing indigenous fish that survives in low-oxygen ponds. Faster-growing Thai and Vietnamese strains introduced mid-2000s catalysed a rapid expansion of commercial koi farming in Mymensingh and northern Bangladesh. Consumed live, commands premium prices.

sources.title: Sarker et al. 2015, Proc. Zool. Soc.
Rahman et al. 2022, Aquaculture, Fish and Fisheries

technologies.name: Shing / Magur (catfishes)
technologies.developer: Indigenous South Asian air-breathing catfishes; induced breeding tech by BFRI and BAU from 1980s; hybrid magur introduced in 1990s
technologies.description: Air-breathing indigenous catfishes prized for flavour, high iron content and perceived medicinal value, fetching some of the highest pond-fish prices in Bangladesh. Can be cultured at high densities in shallow ponds with little dissolved oxygen. Hybrid magur (with exotic C. gariepinus) is widespread despite invasiveness concerns.

sources.title: Mahalder et al. 2025, Aquaculture, Fish and Fisheries

technologies.name: Excavated homestead pond aquaculture
technologies.developer: Department of Fisheries (DoF) with WorldFish technical support and donor-funded extension (Danida MAEP, USAID)
technologies.description: Construction and management of small (0.05-0.2 ha) excavated earthen ponds at the homestead for stocking carp polyculture. From the mid-1980s onward, large-scale extension converted derelict water bodies into productive aquaculture ponds, contributing to a near tripling of pond aquaculture output between 1990 and 2000.

sources.title: Belton et al. 2011 Review of aquaculture and fish consumption

technologies.name: Supplementary fish feed (pelleted)
technologies.developer: Private feed mills (Quality, Mega, Saudi-Bangla, Nourish, ACI Godrej) with technical guidance from WorldFish, DoF and BFRI
technologies.description: Pelleted (and earlier farm-made) compound feeds from rice bran, oilcakes, fishmeal, soy, vitamin/mineral premixes. Adoption accelerated after 2000; the share of farms using formulated feeds rose from 43 to 69 percent over an eight-year period. Trade-offs include high feed cost (60-70 percent of variable cost), pressure on marine fishmeal supplies, and antimicrobial-resistance concerns.

technologies.name: Induced spawning of carps (GnRH / HCG)
technologies.developer: BFRI, DoF, university hatcheries; synthetic analogues (Ovaprim, Wova-FH, HCG)
technologies.cgiar_origin: WorldFish supported genetic improvement and hatchery extension
technologies.description: Hypophysation and synthetic-hormone induction (carp pituitary, HCG, salmon-GnRH-analogue products such as Ovaprim) used to spawn Indian and Chinese major carps that do not breed naturally in ponds. Underpins essentially all carp seed production in Bangladesh's ~900 hatcheries.

sources.title: FAO seed production of carps manual
Asian Fisheries Society Hormones and Spawning

technologies.name: Tilapia sex reversal (monosex tilapia)
technologies.developer: WorldFish (GIFT program) with BFRI, DoF and private hatcheries (BRAC, Fishtech)
technologies.description: Oral administration of feed treated with 17 alpha-methyltestosterone (50-80 mg/kg feed for 21-28 days) to first-feeding fry produces nearly all-male populations that grow faster and avoid prolific in-pond reproduction. Combined with GIFT-derived strains, mono-sex tilapia is the basis of Bangladesh's tilapia boom (>400,000 t/yr).

technologies.name: Pond disease control (lime, KMnO4, biosecurity)
technologies.developer: DoF, BFRI fish-health labs, WorldFish biosecurity projects, private aqua-drug suppliers
technologies.description: Routine application of agricultural lime for pH and pathogen control, potassium permanganate, bleaching powder, salt, and antibiotics (oxytetracycline, ciprofloxacin) to manage EUS, motile Aeromonas septicaemia, parasites and saprolegniasis. Surveys find ~99 percent of farmers use disinfectants regularly and ~21 percent use antibiotics. Trade-offs: antimicrobial resistance, residues in fish, fish-kill from KMnO4 overdose.

technologies.name: Mechanical aeration and water exchange
technologies.developer: Private commercial farms with BFRI, BAU and WorldFish technical input
technologies.description: Paddlewheel, blower, and aspirator aerators plus periodic pump-driven water exchange maintain dissolved oxygen above ~3 mg/L in intensive pangas, tilapia and koi ponds. Aerated ponds maintain DO ~7 mg/L versus ~2 mg/L in non-aerated ponds, allowing several-fold higher stocking densities and yields.

technologies.name: Cage culture in open water
technologies.developer: WorldFish (CARE-Bangladesh CAGES project), BFRI, DoF and private operators in Dakatia, Meghna and Kaptai systems
technologies.description: Floating or fixed mesh cages (1-50 m3) stocked with mono-sex tilapia, pangas or Thai silver barb in rivers, beels and reservoirs, providing landless and near-landless households with access to aquaculture without owning ponds. Cage production grew ~2.5 fold between 2014 and 2022 to ~5,000 t/yr. Trade-offs: conflict with capture fisheries, nutrient loading, theft losses.

technologies.name: Two-stage nursery and grow-out
technologies.developer: BFRI Freshwater Station and FAO/UNDP Aquaculture Development Project, scaled with WorldFish and DoF
technologies.cgiar_origin: WorldFish technical support and fingerling-quality research
technologies.description: Separation of the cycle into nursery (rearing spawn to fingerlings ~8-12 cm) and grow-out phases. The system raises survival from less than 10 percent (direct spawn stocking) to over 70 percent and is standard for private hatcheries and open-water stocking programs (~400-500 million fingerlings released annually).

sources.title: FAO large size carp fingerling production

technologies.name: Integrated rice-fish farming
technologies.developer: BRRI, BFRI, DoF and WorldFish; NGO scale-up by CARE, BRAC, Practical Action
technologies.description: Concurrent or rotational culture of carps, tilapia or climbing perch in rice fields modified with perimeter trenches and refuges, including the saline-coastal gher variant. Trials show simultaneous rice yield gains (5-15 percent) and supplementary fish output (200-500 kg/ha), with reduced pesticide use.

technologies.name: Integrated duck-fish / poultry-fish farming
technologies.developer: BFRI with FAO technical assistance and DoF extension
technologies.description: Khaki Campbell ducks (or layer/broiler chickens) housed over or adjacent to carp polyculture ponds; droppings fertilise the pond, eliminating chemical fertilizer or supplementary feed. Field trials show 4-5 t/ha/yr fish yield at 400-500 ducks/ha versus ~0.5 t/ha for unmanaged ponds.

sources.title: FAO polyculture and integrated fish farming

technologies.name: Carp-mola polyculture (nutrition-sensitive)
technologies.developer: WorldFish (Thilsted et al.) with BFRI, BAU and DoF
technologies.description: Polyculture of major carps with mola (Amblypharyngodon mola), a small indigenous species rich in vitamin A, iron, zinc and calcium consumed whole. Adding mola to existing carp ponds raises micronutrient intake of women and young children without reducing total pond income.

sources.title: WorldFish small indigenous fish in Bangladesh
Sarkar et al. 2023, Frontiers in Aquaculture

technologies.name: Four-wheel tractor
technologies.developer: Imported from Indian, Chinese, Japanese and Western manufacturers (Mahindra, Sonalika, Kubota, John Deere)
technologies.cgiar_origin: CIMMYT and CSISA evaluated 4WT-mounted conservation-agriculture implements
technologies.description: Four-wheel tractors provide higher-horsepower tillage for medium-to-large farms and transport. Minority of the tractor fleet in Bangladesh (dominated by 2WT power tillers) but expanding through subsidised purchase under the Agricultural Mechanization Project and service-provider business models.

sources.title: Mottaleb, Krupnik & Erenstein 2016, J Rural Studies 46

technologies.name: Two-wheel power tiller
technologies.developer: Originated with Japanese (Kubota, Yanmar, Honda) and Chinese (Dongfeng, Sifang) manufacturers. Mass adoption followed Bangladesh's 1988-89 import liberalisation; CIMMYT and CSISA-MI supported attached implements.
technologies.description: Bangladesh's dominant tillage machine, used on roughly 80 percent of cultivated land. Replaced animal draft, enabling timely tillage between rice crops and supporting the boom in Boro rice. The engine also serves as a prime mover for threshers, pumps, seeders and transport.

technologies.name: Power thresher
technologies.developer: BRRI Farm Machinery and Post-Harvest Technology Division (open-drum and closed-drum threshers adapted from IRRI prototypes); local manufacturers in Bogra and Jessore
technologies.cgiar_origin: IRRI thresher designs adapted by BRRI
technologies.description: Power threshers separate paddy grain from straw using a rotating spike-tooth or wire-loop drum driven by a diesel engine or power-tiller take-off. BRRI-designed open-drum threshers dramatically reduced threshing time and post-harvest losses compared to manual beating.

sources.title: BRRI innovations local agro machine industry (TBS)

technologies.name: Treadle (pedal) thresher
technologies.developer: Foot-operated wire-loop threshers introduced and adapted by BRRI and extension agencies, drawing on Japanese and IRRI designs from the 1960s
technologies.cgiar_origin: Based on IRRI/Japanese designs adapted by BRRI
technologies.description: Foot-pedalled wire-loop drum used by smallholders to thresh paddy without an engine. Bridged the gap between manual beating and engine-driven threshers in the 1970s-80s and remains in use where farms are too small or remote to justify a power thresher.

technologies.name: Combine harvester
technologies.developer: Imported mini and full-size combines from China (World, Wubota), Japan (Kubota, Yanmar) and Korea (Daedong). BRRI Farm Machinery Division has also designed a head-feed mini combine.
technologies.cgiar_origin: CSISA-MI and CIMMYT support service-provider deployment
technologies.description: Self-propelled combine harvesters cut, thresh and clean rice or wheat in one operation. Uptake accelerated rapidly after 2018 once the Agricultural Mechanization Project began providing 50-70 percent subsidies (50 percent in plains, 70 percent in haor and coastal regions). Combines have become the principal response to seasonal labour shortages.

technologies.name: Motorised reaper
technologies.developer: Chinese self-propelled reapers and BRRI-designed reaper attachments for 2WT; CSISA-MI supported localisation and service-provider networks
technologies.cgiar_origin: CIMMYT / CSISA-MI scale-up; BRRI design adaptations
technologies.description: Walk-behind or 2WT-mounted machines that cut standing paddy or wheat and lay it in a windrow for separate threshing. BRRI evaluations show a self-propelled reaper covers ~0.25 ha/hr versus 0.004 ha/hr by hand, cutting labour from ~248 to ~68 man-hours/ha. Lower-cost entry than combines for smaller service providers.

technologies.name: PTOS / strip-till seeder / bed planter
technologies.developer: Originally a Chinese 2WT seeder; refined for Bangladesh by CIMMYT, CSISA, CSISA-MI and local manufacturers (Janata Engineering, Alim Industries)
technologies.description: The power-tiller-operated seeder (PTOS) and its strip-till and bed-planter variants attach to a 2WT to till, place seed and fertiliser, cover seed and level soil in a single pass. They underpin conservation-agriculture practice, cutting establishment costs by ~67 percent and reducing irrigation time.

technologies.name: Motorised / battery knapsack sprayer
technologies.developer: Imported from China and India; battery-powered models from Chinese and local manufacturers
technologies.description: Engine and battery-powered knapsack sprayers deliver pesticides and foliar fertilisers more uniformly and faster than lever-operated sprayers. Battery sprayers have spread rapidly since the mid-2010s under the Agricultural Mechanization Project's machinery list.

technologies.name: Mechanical rice transplanter
technologies.developer: IRRI 6-row manual transplanter modified by BRRI in 2000; self-propelled riding/walking transplanters from Korea (Daedong/Kukje), Japan (Kubota, Yanmar) and China from 2009 onward
technologies.cgiar_origin: IRRI prototype adapted by BRRI; IRRI community-nursery scaling 2023-2025
technologies.description: Mechanical rice transplanters place mat-raised seedlings in evenly spaced rows, cutting transplanting labour from ~125 to ~10 man-hours per hectare. Adoption remains limited because of high machine cost, the need for specialised mat nurseries, and small plot sizes; IRRI and BRRI now scaling community-nursery models.

sources.title: IRRI Rice Today: Mechanical rice transplanting

technologies.name: Low-lift pump (LLP)
technologies.developer: Imported centrifugal pumpsets distributed by BADC from the early 1960s; design refined locally and by BRRI
technologies.cgiar_origin: Later evaluated against axial-flow pumps by CIMMYT/CSISA
technologies.description: Diesel- or electric-driven centrifugal pumps that lift water a few metres from rivers, khals and ponds to flood-irrigate paddy. Introduced systematically by BADC in the 1960s on a rental basis, they were the first modern irrigation technology in Bangladesh; by 1978 some 35,000 LLPs were operating.

sources.title: Krupnik et al. 2015, Irrigation and Drainage

technologies.name: Axial-flow pump (AFP)
technologies.developer: Introduced to Bangladesh by IRRI; adapted by CIMMYT, CSISA-MI and iDE with local manufacturers (RFL, Janata, Alim Industries). Technical work led by T.J. Krupnik and colleagues.
technologies.cgiar_origin: CGIAR-linked: IRRI design, scaled by CIMMYT/CSISA-MI
technologies.description: Low-head, high-discharge propeller pump optimised for the shallow lifts (1-3 m) typical of Bangladesh's southern delta. Independent testing by Krupnik et al. (2015) showed AFPs can lift up to 55 percent more water per unit fuel than conventional centrifugal pumps at low heads.

technologies.name: Shallow tubewell, diesel pump
technologies.developer: Diesel pumpsets imported mainly from China and India coupled to locally driven shallow tubewells (STWs); BADC initially regulated, privatised after the 1988 liberalisation
technologies.description: Shallow tubewells (typically 6-50 m deep) coupled to small diesel centrifugal pumps unleashed the Boro-rice revolution in Bangladesh after the 1988 liberalisation of minor-irrigation imports. They now irrigate the largest share of the country's dry-season cropped area.

technologies.name: Deep tubewell, electric pump
technologies.developer: Deep tubewells (>75 m, 1-2 cusec discharge) installed by BADC from 1962; mostly electric submersible or turbine pumps driven by REB / BPDB grid power
technologies.description: Deep tubewells with electric submersible or vertical-turbine pumps draw groundwater from deep aquifers and supply command areas of 20-50 ha. Backbone of public-sector irrigation in the 1960s-70s and still important in the Barind tract, increasingly powered by grid or solar PV.

technologies.name: Treadle pump
technologies.developer: Designed by Norwegian engineer Gunnar Barnes with RDRS Bangladesh (1975-79); mass-marketed from 1986 by iDE through a network of ~84 local manufacturers
technologies.description: Foot-operated twin-cylinder suction pump that lifts shallow groundwater (up to ~7 m) for irrigating small plots. More than 1.5 million units sold in Bangladesh, generating an estimated USD 1.4 billion in net annual income for smallholders.

technologies.name: Rower pump
technologies.developer: Developed by Mirpur Agricultural Workshop and Training School (MAWTS) and partners in the early 1980s as a low-cost alternative to the treadle pump
technologies.description: Hand-operated reciprocating suction pump using a horizontal lever like a rowing motion. Cheaper and easier to install than a treadle pump, well-suited to homestead gardens and very small plots.

technologies.name: Satabdi / BARI Gom 21
technologies.developer: BARI Wheat Research Centre with CIMMYT germplasm
technologies.type: Leaf blight and leaf rust tolerant wheat
technologies.description: Leaf blight and leaf rust tolerant wheat released in 2000, one of the early disease tolerant varieties addressing chronic foliar disease problems in Bangladeshi wheat.

technologies.name: BARI Gom 25 (salt tolerant)
technologies.developer: BARI Wheat Research Centre with CIMMYT
technologies.description: Salt tolerant wheat developed jointly by BARI Wheat Research Centre and CIMMYT, targeting the saline coastal belt where wheat is increasingly grown as a rabi crop.

technologies.name: BARI Gom 27 (Ug99 tolerant)
technologies.developer: BARI Wheat Research Centre with CIMMYT under CSISA
technologies.description: Ug99 tolerant wheat released in 2008 under the BARI WRC and CIMMYT partnership, part of the CSISA programme's preemptive breeding response to Ug99, the African stem rust strain threatening South Asian wheat.

technologies.name: BARI Gom 33 (blast resistant, Zn enriched)
technologies.developer: BARI with CIMMYT and HarvestPlus
technologies.type: Blast resistant and zinc biofortified wheat
technologies.description: Released in 2017 after the 2016 wheat blast outbreak. Blast resistant and zinc enriched, the first variety to combine the two traits.

technologies.name: BARI Hybrid Maize 3 (protein enriched)
technologies.developer: BARI with CIMMYT
technologies.description: Quality protein maize (QPM) hybrid released in 2002 to address protein malnutrition through staple food enrichment.

technologies.name: BARI Hybrid Maize 14 (heat tolerant)
technologies.developer: BARI with CIMMYT under Heat Tolerant Maize for Asia (HTMA)
technologies.description: Heat tolerant maize hybrid released in 2017 under the Heat Tolerant Maize for Asia (HTMA) project, BARI and CIMMYT collaborators.

technologies.name: BARI Hybrid Maize 16 (salt tolerant)
technologies.developer: BARI single-crossed a hybrid selected from a CIMMYT trial
technologies.description: Salt tolerant maize hybrid produced by BARI single-crossing a hybrid selected from a CIMMYT trial.

technologies.name: BARI ALU 22 (SAIKAT, saline tolerant)
technologies.developer: BARI Tuber Crops Research Centre (TCRC) with CIP
technologies.description: Salt tolerant potato bred for the coastal saline belt, jointly developed with CIP.

technologies.name: BARI ALU 46 (late blight resistant)
technologies.developer: BARI TCRC with CIP under the Root and Tuber Crops R&D Programme
technologies.description: Late blight resistant potato released in 2013, addressing the most damaging fungal disease of the Bangladeshi potato crop.

technologies.name: BARI ALU 73 (heat tolerant)
technologies.developer: BARI TCRC with CIP
technologies.description: Heat tolerant potato released in 2016 to extend the potato growing window in a warming climate.

technologies.name: BARI SP 12 / 13 (orange fleshed)
technologies.developer: BARI TCRC with CIP, Scaling Up Sweetpotato Through Agriculture and Nutrition (SUSTAIN) programme
technologies.description: Beta-carotene rich orange-fleshed sweetpotato released in 2013 under the CIP SUSTAIN programme to address widespread vitamin A deficiency, particularly among children.

technologies.name: BARI SP 14 / 15 (orange fleshed)
technologies.developer: BARI TCRC with CIP under SUSTAIN
technologies.description: Second generation orange-fleshed sweetpotatoes released in 2017 to expand the geographic reach of biofortified sweetpotato in Bangladesh.

technologies.name: BARI Masur 4 (stemphylium blight resistant, Zn enriched)
technologies.developer: BARI with ICARDA; later iterations involved HarvestPlus from 2010
technologies.description: Stemphylium blight resistant lentil, also micronutrient enriched (Zn and Fe). Foundation of the BARI Masur series of CGIAR-linked biofortified lentils.

technologies.name: BARI Masur 8 (Zn/Fe biofortified)
technologies.developer: BARI with ICARDA and HarvestPlus
technologies.description: Zinc and iron biofortified lentil released in 2015 with HarvestPlus support, building on the disease tolerant Masur series.

technologies.name: BINA Masur 10 (drought tolerant)
technologies.developer: BINA with ICARDA
technologies.description: Drought tolerant lentil targeting the North Western drought prone districts of Bangladesh, released in 2016.

technologies.name: BARI Chinabadam 6 (short duration)
technologies.developer: BARI with ICRISAT
technologies.description: Short duration groundnut variety released in 1998, first of the ICRISAT-linked groundnut releases in Bangladesh.

technologies.name: BARI Chinabadam 7 (high yielding)
technologies.developer: BARI with ICRISAT
technologies.description: High yielding groundnut variety from ICRISAT germplasm, released in 2004.

technologies.name: BARI Chola 5 (high yielding)
technologies.developer: BARI with ICRISAT
technologies.description: High yielding chickpea variety released in 1996 from the BARI-ICRISAT partnership.

technologies.name: BARI Chola 10 (heat tolerant)
technologies.developer: BARI with ICRISAT
technologies.description: Heat tolerant chickpea released in 2017 to adapt the crop to warming Bangladeshi conditions.

technologies.name: G3 rohu (genetically improved rohu)
technologies.developer: WorldFish Rohu Genetic Improvement Program (CGIP)
technologies.description: Generation 3 rohu from the WorldFish Rohu Genetic Improvement Program (CGIP), released to Bangladesh hatcheries in 2020. On farm trials in 2022 at 19 hatcheries in Jashore, Natore and Rajshahi showed G3 rohu weighing 37 percent more than unimproved strains. By 2023 over 30 commercial hatcheries and 24 nurseries were supplying G3 rohu seed.

technologies.name: Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD)
technologies.developer: BRRI, BRAC, and IRRI; later expanded through DAE and Barind Multipurpose Development Authority (BMDA)
technologies.description: Water management practice in irrigated rice that can significantly reduce methane emissions and water use. The first AWD trial in Bangladesh was conducted in 2004 by BRRI and BRAC with IRRI support; formal extension promotion began in the 2010 Boro season with 50,000 PVC field water tubes distributed across six northwestern districts.

sources.title: Stevenson et al. on AWD methodology

technologies.name: Rice Crop Manager (RCM)
technologies.developer: IRRI and CSISA under the CGIAR Research Program on Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security (CCAFS)
technologies.description: Online tool where farmers answer questions about their plot and management and receive site specific nutrient and management recommendations. Builds on IRRI's earlier work on Site-Specific Nutrient Management (SSNM).

technologies.name: Macher Gari (digital fish marketing)
technologies.developer: WorldFish with private sector and Local Extension Agents for Fisheries (LEAFs)
technologies.description: Digital marketplace for fish farmers in southwest Bangladesh. Project administrative data suggest 50,000+ fish farmers reached, with 200 input retailers and ~100 LEAFs using the platform.

technologies.name: Right Haat (digital input marketplace)
technologies.developer: WorldFish, with input retailer and LEAF network
technologies.description: Digital input marketplace linking smallholder aquaculture farmers, input retailers and Local Extension Agents for Fisheries in southwest Bangladesh.

technologies.name: Index based flood insurance
technologies.developer: WorldFish under the CGIAR Research Program on Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security (CCAFS)
technologies.description: CGIAR worked on index based insurance in Bangladesh through WorldFish's role in CCAFS. The MIXTAPE survey instrument asks households about awareness of crop and livestock insurance and participation in index based flood insurance schemes.
